name: Letrozole

track.title: Lab & animal
track.line: Mouse and rat studies on the label

track.title: Phase III
track.line: BIG 1-98, MA-17 and others, in women

what.text: Letrozole is a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor taken by mouth. Aromatase is the enzyme that turns androgens (androstenedione and testosterone) into estrogens (estrone and estradiol). Letrozole binds the enzyme and blocks it, which lowers estrogen in all tissues.
How it acts, according to the FDA label and studies in men:

items.text: In women it lowers estrone, estradiol and estrone sulfate. It has no significant effect on cortisol-type hormones, aldosterone or thyroid hormones.
In men, lower estradiol weakens estrogen’s brake on the pituitary, so LH and testosterone rise. Studies in obese men and in infertile men measured this.

src.label: Loves et al., Eur J Endocrinol
Sun et al., JAMA Netw Open

what.text: Letrozole is approved only for breast cancer in postmenopausal women. Its use in men, for example to raise testosterone or for infertility, is off-label.

research.text: Femara was approved on large trials in postmenopausal women with breast cancer. In men, studies are small: a 12-man pilot and a 42-man placebo-controlled trial in obese men with low testosterone, and a 296-man randomized trial in men with severe infertility. Hormones changed clearly; symptoms and body measures did not in the placebo-controlled trial.

research.title: Weekly letrozole in severely obese men (Loves et al.)

facts.v: 12 severely obese men (BMI over 35) with low testosterone from the pituitary
estradiol, LH, total and free testosterone

research.found: After 6 weeks, estradiol fell by about half, LH rose from 4.4 to 11.1 U/L and total testosterone from 5.9 to 19.6 nmol/L. Free testosterone rose above the normal range in 7 of the 12 men. Levels stayed stable over 6 months.

src.label: Loves et al., Eur J Endocrinol

research.title: Letrozole vs placebo in obese men with low testosterone (Loves et al.)

facts.v: 42 obese men (BMI over 35) with total testosterone under 10 nmol/L; 39 completed
letrozole starting at 2.5 mg a week, increased monthly toward a testosterone target, or placebo
mood and psychological function, body composition, exercise capacity, glucose, lipids and bone

research.found: Estradiol fell from 119 to 59 pmol/L and total testosterone rose from 8.6 to 21.5 nmol/L. None of the planned clinical endpoints changed significantly.

src.label: Loves et al., Eur J Endocrinol

research.title: Letrozole in men with spermatogenic failure (Sun et al.)

facts.v: multicenter, open-label, assessor-blinded randomized trial at 10 centers (ChiCTR2300073861)
296 men, mean age 30, with no sperm from testicular failure, very few sperm, or severe low counts; 74% had no sperm
letrozole 2.5 mg a day plus vitamins C and E (147 men), or vitamins C and E alone (149)
share of men moving up a WHO sperm concentration category; semen; hormones

research.found: 14.3% on letrozole vs 5.4% on control moved up a sperm concentration category. LH, FSH and testosterone rose and estradiol fell. Semen measures did not differ between groups. Lower libido was more common on letrozole (12.2% vs 5.4%).

src.label: Sun et al., JAMA Netw Open

research.text: The label’s trials, such as BIG 1-98 (letrozole vs tamoxifen) and MA-17 (letrozole vs placebo after tamoxifen), enrolled postmenopausal women with breast cancer. These results do not tell us about effects in men.

In male animals, letrozole may impair fertility, according to the label. In young male rats it caused testicular damage and lower fertility that did not reverse at clinically relevant exposures. In mice and rats it increased benign ovarian tumors.

us.text: Letrozole is FDA approved, as Femara since July 25, 1997, for breast cancer in postmenopausal women. Every approved use is in postmenopausal women; use in men is off-label. It is not a controlled substance. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: NDA 020726 (Novartis), approved July 25, 1997, still marketed. Generic letrozole tablets are also approved.

add-on (adjuvant) treatment of hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer; extended adjuvant treatment after 5 years of tamoxifen; and first- and second-line treatment of advanced breast cancer. All are in postmenopausal women.
off-label. Men are not in any approved indication. The label says safety and effectiveness have not been established in children.

under section 503A, pharmacies may compound only with bulk substances that meet a USP or NF monograph, are part of an FDA-approved drug, or are on FDA’s 503A bulks list. Letrozole is the active ingredient of FDA-approved Femara. A compounded letrozole product is not FDA approved.

world.lead: Letrozole is an approved breast cancer medicine in the US, Canada, Northern Ireland and all 27 EU member states, for postmenopausal women. Use in men is off-label wherever checked. It is banned in sport at all times.

after.text: Australia’s Poisons Standard (October 2026) lists letrozole in Schedule 4 (prescription only). The TGA’s register could not be reached to confirm which products are registered.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Letrozole is named under class S4.1, aromatase inhibitors, on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List. S4 is prohibited at all times (in and out of competition), and S4.1 substances are Specified Substances. The ban is not limited to men. Letrozole stays named in S4.1 on the 2027 list, in force January 1, 2027.

side.text: The label’s side effects come from trials in postmenopausal women: bone loss and fractures, higher cholesterol, hot flushes, joint pain, fatigue and dizziness, with rare serious skin, allergic and liver reactions. In men, a 2026 trial found lower libido more often on letrozole, and a pilot study found free testosterone above the normal range in most men.

items.text: lumbar spine bone density fell a median 4.1% at 24 months on letrozole vs a 0.3% rise on tamoxifen. In BIG 1-98, fractures occurred in 14.7% vs 11.4%; in MA-17, 13.3% vs 7.8% on placebo.
raised cholesterol was reported in 52.3% on letrozole vs 28.6% on tamoxifen in BIG 1-98.
hot flushes (33.5%), joint pain or arthritis (25.4%), night sweats, weight gain, nausea, fatigue and muscle pain. The label warns that fatigue, dizziness and sleepiness can affect driving.

after approval: liver enzyme rises and hepatitis, allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, angioedema, toxic epidermal necrolysis, erythema multiforme, tendon rupture and trigger finger, and blurred vision.
lower libido in 12.2% vs 5.4% on control in the 2026 infertility trial. In the 2008 pilot, free testosterone rose above the normal range in 7 of 12 obese men.
